The Two-striped mabuya (Varzea bistriata) is a diurnal skink found across the Amazon and Atlantic forest biomes, where it occupies shaded forest floor microhabitats with abundant leaf litter. Field measurements indicate that neonatal individuals emerge with a snout-vent length of approximately 3.9 cm [Lb = approximately 3.9 cm], a size that reflects the constraints of the parchment-shelled egg's finite yolk supply. This modest SVL at birth is coupled with a corresponding wet weight of 1.33 g [Wwb = 1.33 g], positioning the species within the typical range for small-bodied Neotropical skinks. Captive incubation studies conducted at a constant 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C] revealed that egg development is completed in approximately 129 days [ab = approximately 129 days], whereas longer developmental periods exceeding 300 days have been noted for wild nests, presumably influenced by lower and more variable natural thermal regimes. The relatively large yolk investment per egg, inferred from the birth mass of 1.33 grams, suggests a substantial maternal energetic commitment that may covary with female body size across populations.

Growth trajectories in this species show pronounced sexual dimorphism in both somatic and reproductive parameters, a pattern common among many Scincidae. Females achieve a larger ultimate snout-vent length of 8.94 cm [Li = 8.94 cm], while males typically reach a maximum SVL of 7.95 cm [Li = 7.95 cm], indicating that females continue somatic expansion over a longer period after the female puberty threshold is crossed. The onset of gonadal maturation in females occurs when individuals attain a snout-vent length of 5.5 cm [Lp = 5.5 cm], a size that is reached well before female asymptotic length. In contrast, males initiate sexual maturation only upon reaching a larger relative size, with puberty first detected at a snout-vent length of 7.2 cm [Lp = 7.2 cm]. This proximate delay in male maturation may be linked to the energetic demands of territory acquisition or intrasexual combat, behaviors that are size-dependent in many congeneric mabuyas and that require extensive somatic growth before reproductive activity can begin.

Reproductive females exhibit substantial seasonal investment in offspring production, consistent with their role as capital breeders. The maximum wet weight recorded for a fully grown, gravid female reaches 16.49 g [Wwi = 16.49 g], a considerable body mass that supports the production of multiple, relatively large eggs per clutch. In contrast, mature males attain an ultimate wet weight of 11.04 g [Wwi = 11.04 g], reflecting a leaner body composition dedicated primarily to somatic maintenance and locomotory performance. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism in mass likely influences the species' life history scheduling, with females allocating a greater proportion of their annual energy budget to reproduction. Even though the species is viviparous, the initial mass of a newborn, at 1.33 g [Wwb = 1.33 g]rams, represents roughly 8 percent of the female's asymptotic mass, a ratio that aligns with the reproductive strategy of many small, forest-dwelling skinks.

Longevity records for this species, derived from captive individuals maintained under controlled thermal conditions, reveal a maximum lifespan of approximately 14.6 years [am = approximately 14.6 years] when kept at a constant temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, for a lizard of this body size, suggests a slow-to-moderate life history pace, potentially buffered by the species' secretive, forest-floor sheltering behavior which reduces predation risk. The age at birth, recorded as 129 days [ab = 129 days] at the same 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C] regime, marks the end of a long gestational period relative to temperate-zone skinks. Field observations, however, indicate that free-ranging females experience gestation periods closer to 300 days, a difference that underscores the powerful effect of environmental temperature on embryonic development rates in this tropical ectotherm. The reproductive output from a single clutch is typically modest, with females laying a small number of eggs that each require substantial maternal provisioning.

Comparative life-history analysis across South American mabuyas shows that Varzea bistriata occupies an intermediate position along the slow-fast continuum, balancing delayed maturation in males with a relatively high reproductive investment per event. The female puberty threshold of 5.5 cm [Lp = 5.5 cm] is reached at an earlier absolute size than the male threshold of 7.2 cm [Lp = 7.2 cm], yet both values fall within the range observed for similarly sized Neotropical skinks. The maximum body mass for females at 16.49 g [Wwi = 16.49 g] and for males at 11.04 g [Wwi = 11.04 g] provides a clear physical basis for the observed sex-specific differences in space use and foraging mode. Individuals that survive to the oldest documented age of 14.6 years [am = 14.6 years] under optimal captive conditions at 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C] likely experience a gradual decline in reproductive output during their final years, a senescence pattern consistent with many long-lived squamates that continue growing throughout life.
